name: Vilnius University
label: Vilnius University
camera_source: Commons cluster (20 photos). Moved 67 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 120 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/531948359: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vilnius University' (307 m across).
notes: One of the oldest universities in Northern Europe, with arcaded courtyards.

text.description: Vilnius University is the oldest and largest university in Lithuania, and on the map it works as a whole cluster of university grounds rather than a single building. The outline of the site is about 300 metres across, so there is plenty to explore on foot. It was founded in 1579 as the Jesuit Academy of Vilnius by Stephen Báthory, which makes it one of the older universities in Central and Eastern Europe. It was closed after the failed November Uprising of 1830–1831 and did not reopen until 1919. Today more than 23,000 students study here, and the university also runs a library, a museum and botanical gardens. For a phone photographer the appeal is the sense of age and scale: long façades, passages and open courtyards where you can include people walking through to show size. Take a few wide frames to set the scene, then move closer for doors, windows, stonework and signs. Walk slowly and look for places where one building frames another. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep vertical walls straight, and check for passing students or visitors before you press the shutter. This is a working university, so respect any signs and access rules.
text.geographic_location: In Vilnius, Lithuania's capital, where the university buildings and grounds spread over an area about 300 metres across.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want a whole façade or courtyard in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details and for pulling distant doorways or windows closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (inside the Grand Courtyard, facing the St John's Church facade and bell tower). The church facade and bell tower framed by the arcaded courtyard, with the observatory tower and its zodiac frieze in view. Walk a little closer along the way to find clean frames of the façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Include an archway, passage or a person at the edge of the frame to give a sense of scale. Take one wide shot and one close detail shot of each part you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so pale stonework keeps its texture and the sky does not wash out. In shaded courtyards, tap on a darker area instead and let the phone brighten the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Soft overcast days also suit the walls and courtyards well.

text.access_note: This is a working university, so respect any signs and access rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The site includes courtyards, passages and long façades that suit photography.
Some areas of a working university may have access rules.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Overcast light suits stonework and courtyards.

name: Gediminas' Tower
label: Gediminas' Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/325130082: the OpenStreetMap point 'Vilnius Upper Castle'.
notes: Remaining tower of the Upper Castle with views over the Old Town.

text.description:
Gediminas' Tower is the surviving part of the Upper Castle, standing on top of Gediminas Hill above Vilnius Old Town. It is a short, sturdy brick tower of three storeys, and it has become a symbol of both the city and Lithuania. It appeared on the old litas currency, and the national flag was raised on it again on 7 October 1988. The first wooden fortifications here are linked to Grand Duke Gediminas, and the first brick castle was finished in 1409 under Grand Duke Vytautas. The tower you see today was rebuilt in 1933.

It photographs well for two reasons. The tower itself makes a strong, simple shape against the sky, and the hilltop gives you a lift above the rooftops of the Old Town. The viewing platform also looks towards the modern business district, so one visit gives you both an old and a new Vilnius in the frame.

The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, so this is the place for close shots of the brickwork and the walls, and for looking out from the hill. Take a few steps back along the hilltop to fit the whole tower in, then go up to the platform for the panorama. Wipe your lens first, as phones pick up smudges easily, and keep your thumb clear of the edges when shooting wide.
text.geographic_location: Gediminas' Tower stands on top of Gediminas Hill in Vilnius, overlooking the Old Town. The rebuilt Royal Palace of Lithuania is near the base of the hill.
text.directions_text: Head for Gediminas Hill in Vilnius, close to the Royal Palace of Lithuania at its foot. The hilltop can be reached on foot or by lift, so choose whichever suits you. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for close shots looking up at the tower. Use the default lens (1x) for the tower with some sky around it and for general views from the hilltop. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Old Town roofs and towers from the platform.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tower is right beside you, so you can shoot its walls and the view out over the city. For a full-length shot of the tower, step back along the hilltop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower's vertical edges parallel to the vertical grid lines. When shooting upwards, don't tilt the phone too far, or the walls will lean inwards. From the platform, put the Old Town rooftops in the lower third and leave the sky above. Choose one clear subject, such as a spire or a distant street, rather than trying to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. For the wide view over the city, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer, warmer light on the brick. Earlier in the day or on weekdays the hilltop is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The tower houses a museum and the hilltop can be reached on foot or by lift, so check the official site before you go for access to the tower and the viewing platform.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon and early evening light is usually softer and warmer for photographs.
The hilltop is likely to be busier in the middle of the day and in summer.
The walk up the hill is uphill.

name: Užupis
label: Užupis
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Užupio angelas' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Užupio Angelas' (node/1616746326): point.
notes: Bohemian quarter that calls itself an independent republic.

text.description: Užupis is a small, artistic neighbourhood on the far side of the Vilnia River from Vilnius Old Town. Its name means "beyond the river". It covers only about 60 hectares and has around 7,000 residents, nearly 1,000 of them artists. On 1 April 1997 the district declared itself the Republic of Užupis, with its own constitution, and the joke has stuck ever since. For a phone photographer the best first stop is the main square, where the bronze angel stands. It blows a trumpet from the top of an 8.5 m column and was unveiled on 1 April 2002. The sculptor, Romas Vilčiauskas, also made the Užupis Mermaid. The angel is a symbol of the district's revival, and the money for it came from selling miniature copies. The column gives you a clean vertical line, and the square's cafés and buildings add colour and a sense of place. Once you have the angel, walk to Paupio gatvė, where the constitution is fixed to a wall in 23 languages. Article 12, "A dog has the right to be a dog", is one people like to photograph. Tibet Square is a small green square with prayer flags and is a pleasant third shot. Užupis is a place where people live, so keep voices down and use judgement around private courtyards. Expect crowds on 1 April, the district's independence day.
text.geographic_location: Užupis lies in Vilnius, largely within the Old Town's UNESCO World Heritage area, just across the Vilnia River from the main Old Town streets. The angel stands in the district's main square.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops at this spot, so start from Vilnius Old Town and walk across one of the bridges over the Vilnia River into Užupis. The angel is in the main square near the start of the walk into the district. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the angel on its column with the square around it. If you are close to the column and want to include the café fronts, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). To pick out the angel and its trumpet against the sky, use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (stand in the square at the foot of the column, looking up at the angel). The bronze angel with its raised trumpet, on its 8.5 m column, framed by the square's cafés and buildings. The angel stands in the main square nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the column up with one of the vertical lines so it does not lean. Tilt the phone upwards to place the angel in the top third of the frame, with a slice of café fronts below for context. If you also want a straight-on shot of the constitution plaques, go to Paupio gatvė and stand square to the wall so the lettering reads cleanly. Tibet Square, with its prayer flags, is a good alternative viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the angel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the bronze. Wait for people to move out of shot before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the bronze wings catch the light. Avoid 1 April if you want the square to yourself.

text.access_note: The angel stands in an open public square and is free to see, but Užupis is a residential district, so be considerate of residents.

name: Vilnius Cathedral
label: Vilnius Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trijų Kryžių kalnas' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Vilniaus Kreivoji pilis virsta Trijų Kryžių kalnu' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4870323: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral Basilica of St Stanislaus and St Vladislav' (95 m across).
notes: Neoclassical cathedral with a separate bell tower on Cathedral Square.

text.description: Vilnius Cathedral stands on Cathedral Square in the historic centre and is one of Lithuania's most important religious buildings. Its calm, strict Neoclassical look comes from a rebuild that began in the early 1780s under Laurynas Gucevičius and was finished in 1801. The first documented cathedral on the site was consecrated in 1388, so there is a great deal of history under the pale walls. From the Three Crosses hill you look down on it rather than up at it. The cathedral and the Old Town rooftops sit together across the Vilnia valley, which gives a photo with a real sense of place. It is also a free, public view and often quieter than the square itself. The cathedral is fairly small in the frame from here, so decide what the picture is about: the whole skyline, or the cathedral picked out among the roofs. Keep the cathedral off-centre and let the rooftops and trees fill the foreground. If you want the full facade with the free-standing bell tower beside it, Cathedral Square is the alternative, and the Gediminas Tower gives a panorama with the cathedral among the tiled roofs. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the view changes a lot between a wide shot and a close one.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is on Cathedral Square in the historic centre of Vilnius.
text.directions_text: No station, tram stop or other public transport stop is right at this spot. The hill is reached on foot through Kalnų park, so start from the Old Town and walk towards the park. From there go up to the terrace by the Three Crosses monument. Check the map for the exact park entrance before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view of valley, rooftops and cathedral. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the cathedral closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the cathedral very small, so use it only if you want the sky and the hill in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Trijų Kryžių kalnas (the terrace by the Three Crosses monument, on the hill in Kalnų park). The cathedral and Old Town rooftops seen from above, looking down across the Vilnia valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the cathedral on one of the third lines, with rooftops below it and sky above. Keep the horizon level. Use any trees at the edge as a foreground frame, but keep them out of the cathedral itself. For a different angle, try the picture from Cathedral Square, which shows the full facade with the bell tower beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the roofs do not wash out. At 3x or 5x, hold the phone steady with both hands and elbows tucked in, or brace against something stable.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides describe morning light as better from here. Sunrise and sunset are also recommended, and sunset is the classic time.

text.access_note: The hill and Kalnų park are a free public space, but check the official site before you go for the cathedral itself and for the Gediminas Tower, which may have access rules or a fee.

name: Gate of Dawn
label: Gate of Dawn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aušros Vartų gatvė' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/112746030: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gate of Dawn' (28 m across).
notes: The last surviving city gate, with a revered icon of Our Lady.

text.description:
The Gate of Dawn (Aušros vartai) is the only surviving gate of Vilnius's old city wall. It was built between 1503 and 1514 as one of nine gates, and you can still see the firing openings on its outside. Above the arch sits a small chapel holding a 17th-century painting of the Virgin Mary, which many people travel to pray before. Both Lithuanians and Poles hold the place dear.

It photographs well because it is a narrow, tall gate squeezed between pastel buildings, with the chapel window sitting right above the arch. Standing directly under it gives a weaker picture. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. From there the lane's width frames the arch, the window and the vault together, and a portrait-orientation frame suits it best.

Keep to the pavement and keep the entrances clear. Photography is not allowed inside the chapel, and not during services. If you have a few minutes, the Baroque Basilian Monastery Gate nearby makes a second shot, with the Gate of Dawn visible further along the street behind it.
text.geographic_location: The gate stands on Aušros Vartų gatvė in Vilnius, and is the only surviving gate of the former city wall. The Church of St Theresa is right beside it.
text.directions_text: Walk from Vilnius Old Town. The gate is on Aušros Vartų gatvė. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) from up the street. It compresses the lane so the arch and chapel window fill the frame between the buildings. The default lens (1x) works as a wider alternative, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) is best kept for the Basilian Monastery Gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Keep the entrances clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait) so the window and the vault above the arch fit in one image. Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the centre so the buildings on both sides balance. For a different view, go to the Basilian Monastery Gate and put its Baroque gate in the foreground, with the Gate of Dawn further along the street behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the painted details. Wait for a gap in the people passing before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups arrive. One guide says late afternoon light suits the chapel best.

text.access_note: The gate and street are public, but the chapel is a place of worship where photography is not allowed inside or during services, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and rules.

name: Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania
label: Grand Dukes' Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trijų kryžių kalnas' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Vilniaus Kreivoji pilis virsta Trijų Kryžių kalnu' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/52710382: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania' (141 m across).
notes: Rebuilt royal residence below Gediminas Hill.

text.description:
The Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania stands in the lower castle area of Vilnius Old Town. It was first built in the 15th century for the rulers of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and was pulled down in 1801. Work on a new palace on the same site began in 2002 and took 16 years, finishing in 2018. The rebuilt palace is in a Renaissance style. It is a large, pale building, and it photographs best as part of the Old Town rather than as a single close-up.

The best view for that is from Trijų kryžių kalnas, the lookout above the Old Town. From there you get a wide panorama in which the palace sits among the cathedral and the other roofs. The walk up is pleasant and part of the appeal. At this distance the palace is one building among many, so the picture is really about the whole skyline. Start wide to show the layout of the Old Town, then zoom in for a tighter shot of the palace and its neighbours.

If you want the palace's facade and arches at street level, Katedros aikštė is the alternative. The cathedral stands beside the palace there. Both spots are outdoors, so a clear day will give you the most detail.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in the lower castle area of Vilnius Old Town, close to the cathedral. The lookout for the main photo, Trijų kryžių kalnas, is on the hill above the Old Town, to the east of the palace.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are given for this spot, so start from Vilnius Old Town and head to Trijų kryžių kalnas. If you would rather see it at street level, walk down to Katedros aikštė beside the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole Old Town panorama, then switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the palace among the roofs. The default lens (1x) is a good middle option.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trijų kryžių kalnas (lookout above the Old Town). A wide panorama of the Old Town where the palace sits among the cathedral and other roofs, suited to a wide-angle phone lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line, so the Old Town roofs fill most of the picture. Take one wide shot with the palace as one part of the scene, then a zoomed shot with the palace on a third. If you want a street-level alternative, Katedros aikštė shows the facade and arches with the cathedral next to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone steady against a rail or wall when you zoom in, as zoomed shots blur more easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, which one guide says gives the city a magical glow.

text.access_note: The lookout and the palace exterior are outdoors. Check the official site before you go to find out whether the hill is free and whether the palace interior is ticketed.

sources.title: Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania

name: Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights
label: KGB Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/427910141: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights'.
notes: Former KGB headquarters turned museum, with prison cells.

text.description:
This is the former KGB headquarters, a large building from 1890 that now houses the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights. Visitors often call it the KGB Museum. It stands across from Lukiškės Square in Vilnius, and its solid, formal frontage makes a strong, serious photo that fits the story it tells.

The building was completed as the court of the Vilna Governorate. Over the next century it was used by several occupying and governing powers. From 1944 until independence was re-established in 1991 it was the KGB's base, with offices, a prison and an interrogation centre. Today it is also a courthouse and holds the Lithuanian Special Archives. The museum itself was established in 1992 and took its current name in 2018.

For a phone photo, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so you are shooting the building from right beside it. Start with the whole frontage, then move in for details such as the windows, doorways and stonework. Because it is a working courthouse and archive as well as a museum, be considerate of people coming and going. Keep your photos respectful of the place and of anyone near the entrance.
text.geographic_location: In Vilnius, directly across from Lukiškės Square.
text.directions_text: Head for Lukiškės Square, which the museum building faces, and look for the large building. If you are coming from another part of the city, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights, also known as the KGB Museum. The phone icon on the map is right at the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole frontage will not fit from the pavement. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the building is right in front of you, so use the wider lens to include the full frontage. Step back along the pavement or towards the square side for a more complete view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them so the walls do not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height to limit the converging-lines effect of ultra-wide. For a second shot, zoom in on one window or doorway and let the stonework fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in soft, even light, such as a bright overcast day, suits the stonework. A quieter time of day also makes it easier to keep the entrance clear of people.

text.access_note: The museum is a visitor attraction in a building that is also a courthouse and archive, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements; the outside can be photographed from the public pavement.

sources.title: Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights

name: Church of St. Anne
label: St. Anne's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bernardinų sodas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bernardinų sodas' (relation/8031046): middle (523 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/387669997: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Anne's Church' (60 m across).
notes: Flamboyant Gothic brick church said to have impressed Napoleon.

text.description: St Anne's is a red-brick Gothic church on the right bank of the Vilnia river, in Vilnius Old Town. The present building went up in 1495–1500 and its outside has changed very little since. The main facade is the star. Pointed arches are framed by rectangular shapes, and the church has a single nave and two towers. The builders used 33 different kinds of clay brick, which gives the red walls a lot of texture for a phone camera to pick up. A well-known legend says Napoleon saw it in 1812 and wished he could carry it home to Paris in the palm of his hand. The church stands beside the much larger Church of St Francis and St Bernardine, and the pair together make a good scene. Most people photograph the front from the street, so the better angle is from Bernardinų sodas, the garden nearby. From there the church rises above the greenery and you can fit both towers in with fewer people around. A second option is Onos aikštė, which shows the whole brick facade and twin towers, with the Bernardine tower behind and Gediminas Hill in the distance. Keep your phone upright to catch the towers, and straighten it with the gridlines so the verticals look true. Photography inside is restricted and flash is not allowed.
text.geographic_location: In Vilnius Old Town, on the right bank of the Vilnia river, right next to the large Church of St Francis and St Bernardine and its monastery.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so walk in from the Old Town. Once you are the church is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot. Walk towards the brick towers and you will reach the front of the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the church above the trees. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the towers are cut off. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brick patterns and the top of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bernardinų sodas (across the street from the church facade). The church rising above the greenery of the garden, which gives a less crowded angle than the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep both towers upright and let the garden's trees fill the lower part of the frame. If you want the full facade face-on, try Onos aikštė, where the Bernardine tower and Gediminas Hill show behind the church. Pilies gatvė gives a street-level view from across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the red brick stays rich. If a lot of sky is in the shot, switch on HDR if your phone offers it. Do not use flash inside the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight suits the brick colour. In summer the church is said to be lit at night, so try night mode then, holding the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public streets and the garden, but the church is a place of worship with restricted photography inside (no flash, permits for professional sessions), so check the official site for opening hours before you go.

name: Three Crosses
label: Hill of Three Crosses
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bernardinų sodas' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bernardinų sodas' (relation/8031046): middle (523 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/325083016: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Hill of the Three Crosses'.
notes: Hilltop monument with a panoramic view of the city.

text.description:
The Three Crosses are three tall white crosses on a wooded hill above Vilnius Old Town, and they have been part of the city's skyline for centuries. Wooden crosses stood here from the early 17th century, and legend links the hill to Franciscan friars who were put to death on it. The wood rotted and the crosses collapsed in 1869. A concrete monument by Antoni Wiwulski followed in 1916, was pulled down in 1950, and was rebuilt in 1989 by Stanislovas Kuzma. The rebuilt crosses stand 1.8 metres taller than the 1916 ones.

From a raised section near the river bank you look over the mature garden trees to the Old Town roofline, with the wooded hill rising behind. The crosses themselves are not the main subject from here. For them, walk up the hill: a small observation deck at the base of the crosses looks out over the Old Town, and the crosses sit in the foreground with the roofs, church spires and Gediminas Tower behind. The climb is steep. Allow time for both views and keep your phone ready as you go.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands on the Hill of Three Crosses in Kalnai Park, overlooking Vilnius Old Town.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so walk from the Old Town towards Bernardinų sodas. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the framed roofline view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the hilltop deck to fit the crosses and the Old Town together. Telephoto (2x-5x) picks out spires and rooftops from either place.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bernardinų sodas (raised section near the Vilnelė river bank, at the foot of the hill). A quieter, framed view of the Old Town roofline above the garden's mature trees, with the wooded hill rising behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From where you stand, let the tree branches frame the roofline and keep the hill behind as a dark backdrop. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. For the classic shot, climb to Trijų Kryžių kalnas and put the three white crosses in the foreground with the roofs, spires and Gediminas Tower behind. Crouch slightly so the crosses stand against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the crosses or the roofline to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white crosses and bright sky keep their detail. On the hilltop, try Live Photos for a moment of movement. If you stay on after dusk, switch to night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or tree.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset suits the hill's west-facing view. If you stay until dusk, take a torch, as the paths are steep, unlit and slippery when wet.

text.access_note: The hill is in a public park, but check the official site before you go for any access changes or path closures.

name: Cathedral Square, Vilnius
label: Cathedral Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stebuklas' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plytelė „Stebuklas“' (node/5167418039): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5361117: 'Grand Duke Gediminas', the best-known feature inside 'Cathedral Square' (316 m across).
notes: The main square of the city at the foot of Castle Hill.

text.description: Cathedral Square (Katedros aikštė) is the main square of Vilnius Old Town, set right in front of the neo-classical cathedral. It is a wide, open space, so you can get the whole cathedral facade and its separate bell tower in one frame. That is easy to do on a phone. The square was laid out in the 19th century, when the cathedral was being rebuilt. Before that, medieval and Renaissance houses stood here, along with parts of the Lower Castle. The paving was renovated in 2000 in light granite, and red granite strips mark the outline of the old castle fortifications. The bell tower stands a few yards from the cathedral, which is unusual outside Italy. Its lower parts are medieval, and the oldest underground section dates from the 13th century. The Gediminas monument by Vytautas Kašuba, unveiled in 1996, is another notable feature of the square. The best photo is taken on Stebuklas, the tile in the middle of the square. It is linked with the Baltic Way human chain, and visitors often step on it and turn around three times to make a wish. With the cathedral and bell tower rising behind it, the tile makes a good foreground for the picture. If you want a bird's-eye view instead, Gediminas Tower and the Three Crosses hill both look over the square. Check the official sites for access before you go.
text.geographic_location: Cathedral Square is in the heart of Vilnius Old Town, directly in front of Vilnius Cathedral, at the crossing of the city's main streets.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and ask for Katedros aikštė (Cathedral Square), the large open square in front of the cathedral. Once you are in the square, walk towards the middle, where the Stebuklas tile is set into the paving. The cathedral and its separate bell tower are easy to spot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the cathedral, the bell tower and the tile together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square around the tile, or if the facade will not fit. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for a tighter shot of the bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the tile in the middle of the square, cathedral behind). The cathedral facade and bell tower behind the tile, which sits in the foreground of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tile in the lower third, with the cathedral and bell tower above it. A friend standing on the tile gives the picture a sense of scale. For a different angle, the view down over the square from Gediminas Tower or from the Three Crosses hill shows the cathedral against the Old Town roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral facade to set focus, then adjust the exposure slider a little if the sky or the stonework looks too bright or too dark. If you take a portrait of a friend on the tile, use portrait mode and check that the cathedral behind them stays recognisable.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when one guide suggests photographing the tile with the cathedral behind it. Earlier in the morning is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the bell tower and Gediminas Tower may be ticketed, so check the official sites before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Visitors often stand on the Stebuklas tile, so you may need to wait a moment to get a clear frame.
Early morning is likely to be quieter in the square than the middle of the day.

pin_flags: main feature: pin put on Grand Duke Gediminas

name: Pilies Street
label: Pilies Street
camera_source: Commons cluster (6 photos), weak. Moved 13 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 65 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/61148608: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Pilies Street' (26 m long).
notes: Main pedestrian street of the Old Town with cafés and souvenir stalls.

text.description: Pilies Street, which means "Castle Street", is one of the main streets of Vilnius Old Town. It is quite short, running between Cathedral Square and Town Hall Square, so it is easy to fit into a walk. It photographs well because it is full of life. Market traders sell folk art, and souvenir shops offer amber jewellery and linen clothes. Their stalls and doorways give you colour and small details to frame. The street is also where many of the city's festival processions pass, and it is known for the Kaziukas Fair, when folk artists from all over Lithuania come to sell their work. Two notable places are linked to the street: the headquarters of Vilnius University, between Pilies Street and University Street, and the House of the Signatories, where the Declaration of Independence was signed on 16 February 1918. For photos, look for a shot that shows the street as a lively, narrow lane rather than a single building. Wait for a gap in the passers-by, then take a few frames in a row so you can pick the best one. Include a shop front or a stall in the foreground to give the picture depth, and keep the horizon level using the gridlines.
text.geographic_location: Pilies Street is in the Old Town of Vilnius, linking Cathedral Square with Town Hall Square. Vilnius University's headquarters are located between Pilies Street and University Street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed near this spot. Head to the Old Town (Cathedral Square or Town Hall Square) and walk onto Pilies Street. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the buildings on both sides and the stalls in one picture. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as amber jewellery, linen or a stall display.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Walk a few steps closer if you want to fill the frame with the street itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the street along the centre line, so the buildings on each side lead the eye forward. Keep a stall or shop front in the corner of the frame to add depth. Take a wide shot (0.5x or 1x), then a closer one at 2x to simplify the scene. If you want to show the bustle, try a Live Photo and choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the busiest part of the street to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building colours stay rich. Turn on night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing. Portrait mode works well for close-ups of crafts on a stall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually the quietest time for a clean view of the street. Later in the day it is livelier, which suits photos of stalls and people. Festival days and the Kaziukas Fair are busy and colourful, but expect crowds.

text.access_note: Pilies Street is an open public street; for festivals, fairs or special events, check the official site before you go.

name: Town Hall, Vilnius
label: Vilnius Town Hall
camera_source: Commons cluster (15 photos). Moved 25 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/111866535: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vilnius Town Hall' (79 m across).
notes: Neoclassical town hall on Town Hall Square.

text.description: Vilnius Town Hall stands on Rotušės aikštė (Town Hall Square) in the Old Town, at the end of Pilies Street. It is a calm, formal building and works well as a backdrop to the busy square around it. The town hall was first mentioned in 1432 and began as a Gothic building. It was rebuilt many times, and the version you see now is neoclassical, designed by Laurynas Gucevičius in 1799 and unchanged since. Its Gothic cellars survive and can be visited, though you should check the official site before you go. The square has long been the city's place for trade and events. Kaziukas Fair is held here, the main Christmas tree is put up here, and concerts and national celebrations take place here too. That gives you a good chance of catching something lively in the frame. From the phone icon on the map you are close to the building and looking back at it across open ground. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines of the walls stay straight. Wait for a gap between passers-by, or let a few people into the shot to show the scale of the place. If an event or market is on, expect stalls or stages in front of the façade, which can make a good foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Vilnius, on Town Hall Square (Rotušės aikštė) at the end of Pilies Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and walk to the far end of Pilies Street, where it opens into Town Hall Square. The phone icon on the map is on the north-east side of the building, about 1 minute on foot from the middle of the town hall. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the full width of the building in. Use 2x or more for details such as the roofline and the portico.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them so the walls stay upright. Keep the whole façade in view with a little sky above it. Try a second shot at 2x for a tighter, tidier frame that leaves out the edges of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the square. Soft evening light is also pleasant on the building, and a night shot with night mode can work well if the façade is lit.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space; for the cellars or any visit inside the town hall, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter in the square.
Soft evening light suits the building, and the façade may be lit at night.
Stalls or stages may stand in front of the façade during fairs and events.

name: Bernardine Garden
label: Bernardine Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bernardinų sodas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bernardinų sodas' (relation/8031046): middle (523 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8031046: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bernardinai Garden' (525 m across).
notes: Park along the Vilnia river below the Bernardine church.

text.description: Bernardine Garden is a large public park in the middle of Vilnius, with flower beds, a fountain and the Vilnelė river along its edge. For a phone photo, the best place is the main rose garden in the central part of the park. The rose beds fill the foreground and the fountain sits behind them as the centrepiece. In the evening the fountain is lit, which adds a second kind of picture. The park covers over 9 hectares and lies between the Gediminas Tower and the Bernardine Monastery. Bernardine monks laid it out after being invited to Vilnius in 1469. It was closed in 1864, rebuilt later, destroyed in the Second World War, and rebuilt again in the Soviet period and in 2013. Other parts of the park hold a herb garden, a botanic display, a giant chessboard and, in the warm months, sculpture exhibitions. For photos, start low and close to the beds so the flowers lead the eye towards the fountain. Then step back and take a wider shot with the water in the middle. If you have time, walk to the riverside path for the fast, gravelly Vilnelė framed by trees. Belvederio kalnelis, the small hill, offers a view down over the garden and river. It is overgrown with shrubs at present, so the view may be partly blocked outside the flowering season.
text.geographic_location: Bernardine Garden is in Vilnius Old Town, on the left bank of the Vilnelė (Vilnia) river, between the Gediminas Tower and the Bernardine Monastery.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and the foot of the Gediminas Tower, then look for the Bernardine Monastery; the garden lies between the two. Once in the park, follow the main paths to the central rose garden, where the fountain stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole scene of beds and fountain, and the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more) for the fountain jets or a single rose bed.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (main rose garden, central part of the park). The garden's flower beds and rose beds in the foreground, with the lit musical fountain as the central focal point. Look for the fountain and rose beds as you walk in that direction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on a third, with a curve of rose beds leading towards it. Crouch a little so the flowers sit above the lawn and path. For a different view, try Belvederio kalnelis, the small hill, for a look down over the garden and river, or the riverside path for the Vilnelė framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest flowers to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the colours do not wash out. For the lit fountain, use night mode and brace your phone on a ledge or against your body to keep it still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The beds look best in the flowering season. For the lit fountain, go in the evening of a warm-season weekday, when the music and light show runs from 9 pm to 10 pm; check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: Bernardine Garden is a public park; for fountain times and any events or exhibitions, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The rose beds look best in the flowering season, roughly summer.
Softer, lower evening light flatters flowers and water.
Night mode works best if the phone is braced against something steady.
The fountain show times can change, so they should be checked before a visit.

name: Gediminas Avenue
label: Gediminas Avenue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gedimino prospektas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gedimino prospektas' (node/920088477): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Main boulevard of the city, running from the cathedral to Lukiškės Square.

text.description:
Gediminas Avenue is the main street of Vilnius, and it is a good place to show the city as people actually use it. Government buildings, theatres, the national library, shops and cafés all line the same long, straight street. It runs from the Žvėrynas Bridge over the Neris, near the Seimas Palace, to Cathedral Square and the Vilnius Castle Complex, so it links the Old Town with Žvėrynas. The avenue was built in 1836 and has had several names since, including St. George Avenue, Stalin Avenue and Lenin Avenue. It has carried its present name since 1989. The section from the Cathedral to Vincas Kudirka Square was rebuilt before 2003, and more than 100 new trees were planted along it.

The street photographs well because it is long and straight. Looking along it, the buildings on both sides lead the eye to Vilnius Cathedral at the far end. The Art Nouveau facades also make good subjects for closer shots. Turn on gridlines so the street stays straight in the frame, and wait for a gap in the people and traffic. Part of the avenue is closed to traffic in the evenings, which makes it calmer to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Gediminas Avenue is the central street of Vilnius. It runs from Cathedral Square in the Old Town to the Žvėrynas Bridge over the Neris, near the Seimas Palace, and passes Lukiškės Square on the way.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. It is about 1 km west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the facades on both sides. A 2x-3x telephoto, if your phone has one, brings the Cathedral closer at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Gedimino prospektas (a point along the avenue, looking towards the Cathedral). The avenue running in perspective toward the Vilnius Cathedral, with the historic buildings lining both sides. Choose a spot on the pavement with a clear line down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the middle of the street in the centre of the frame and use gridlines to keep the buildings upright. Let the buildings on both sides lead the eye to the Cathedral. For a second shot, move closer to one side and use the telephoto or default lens on a single Art Nouveau facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the middle of the street to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a lamp post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually quieter. In the evening, when traffic is kept off part of the avenue, the street is easier to photograph. With the sun low in the west, the light should fall on the buildings in front of you.

text.access_note: This is an open public street. Keep to the pavement and take care at crossings.

name: Church of St. Peter and St. Paul, Vilnius
label: St. Peter & Paul
camera_source: Commons cluster (22 photos). Moved 24 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 150 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/88534413: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Peter and St. Paul's Church' (67 m across).
notes: Baroque church famous for its thousands of white stucco figures inside.

text.description: The Church of Sts. Peter and Paul is a white Baroque church on a small hill in the Antakalnis neighbourhood of Vilnius, close to the Neris River. It was designed by Jan Zaor of Kraków. Building began on 29 June 1668 and the main work finished in 1676. The founder, Michał Kazimierz Pac, paid for it to mark a victory over the Muscovites, who had occupied Vilnius for six years. Outside, the facade is heavy and richly detailed. It has freestanding columns and two bell towers, round at the bottom and eight-sided at the top. A relief of Mary standing on a cannon sits in the broken pediment. The dome is low, so you only really see it from a distance. That makes the walk up from the west a good time for a wide shot. The church is the centrepiece of a monastery complex of about 1.5 hectares. A thick brick wall 4-5 m high surrounds the churchyard, so close-up views from outside are limited. Inside, around 2,000 white stucco figures cover the walls and ceilings, which is why many visitors come. For a phone, the approach is simple: take one wider shot showing the towers and the hill, then step closer for details such as the pediment, the towers and the entrance. Indoors, work slowly and keep your phone steady. Rules on photography inside can vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The church is in the Antakalnis neighbourhood of Vilnius, on a small rise near the Neris River, on the former main road towards Nemenčinė.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or train stop at this spot, so start from the Antakalnis area of Vilnius and come by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped near the church. Walk east from there towards the towers. The phone icon on the map is about 150 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and its towers. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pediment relief and the tops of the towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside, if photography is allowed, to fit in more of the stucco ceiling.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 150 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the church and its setting should fit in one frame without much zooming. Then walk the short distance closer for detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the towers symmetrical on either side of the frame. Leave a little sky above them. From closer in, tilt the phone up only slightly, or use the telephoto lens, to avoid converging walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stonework keeps its detail. Indoors, hold the phone steady with both hands and use night mode if the scene is dim, but keep it still while the shot is taken.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or an evenly overcast day, tends to suit a white building. Strong midday sun can make the walls glare.

text.access_note: This is a working Roman Catholic church, so opening times, dress expectations and rules on photography inside may apply; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, 146 m west of the church, the church and its towers are visible in a single frame.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or overcast weather, usually flatters a white building; strong midday sun can cause glare.
Rules on photography inside a church can vary, and modest dress is often expected in places of worship.
Phones usually reach the stucco ceiling in a single frame only with the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens.

name: Literatų Street
label: Literatų Street
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4515994589: the OpenStreetMap point 'Literatų street project'.
notes: Alley whose wall is covered with art tributes to writers.

text.description: Literatų Street is a short, narrow lane in Vilnius Old Town, and it photographs well because the walls themselves are the attraction. The street is known for its collection of decorative and artistic plaques honouring writers who lived and worked in Vilnius or had some link with the city and Lithuania. The first pieces went up in 2009, when Vilnius was European Capital of Culture, and the collection has since grown to around 200. Each plaque is different, so the wall becomes a patchwork of shapes, materials and colours. The name Literatų means 'of the literati'. It comes from the printing houses and bookshops that once stood here, or from the poet Adam Mickiewicz, who lived here briefly in 1823. Because the lane is so narrow, you will not get a wide, tidy view with one shot. Think in two steps instead. First take a wider frame that shows the whole wall and the lane running away from you. Then move closer and pick out a few plaques you like. Walk slowly, look at the plaques at eye level and just above, and try one frame that follows the line of the wall into the distance. Visit when it is quiet so that people walking past do not block the view. The street is short, so you can easily see it in a few minutes and pair it with the rest of the Old Town.
text.geographic_location: Literatų Street is in the Old Town of Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. It is a short, narrow street, so it is easy to miss if you are not looking for it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Old Town of Vilnius. From there the plaques are about 1 minute on foot to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the narrow lane and the wall of plaques into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for groups of plaques, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single plaques.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Literatų gatvė (middle of the street, facing the plaque-covered walls). The blue walls densely covered with small writers' plaques and artworks, framed by the narrow street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the wall parallel to the edge of the frame so the lines look straight. For a wider shot, shoot along the wall and let it lead the eye down the lane. For details, step close and fill the frame with two or three contrasting plaques.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a plaque to focus on it, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or a bright wall is washing out the colours. Hold the phone steady with both hands, as the lane can be shady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, or whenever the lane is quiet, so you can shoot the wall without people in front of it.

text.access_note: This is a street in the Old Town, so you can walk along it; check local information before you go if you need details about events or works.

name: Church of St. Catherine, Vilnius
label: St. Catherine Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'S. Moniuškos skveras' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'S. Moniuškos skveras' (way/29360548): middle (90 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/112386499: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Šv. Kotrynos bažnyčia' (66 m across).
notes: Baroque church now used as a concert hall.

text.description:
St Catherine's is a Baroque church in Vilnius Old Town, and its twin towers and richly decorated front make a good phone photo. Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, Hetman of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, founded it in 1618 for Benedictine nuns. After the Great Fire of 1737 the architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz gave it the look it has today. He raised the towers to five storeys and added the ornate pediments, and the facade and towers carry Rococo decoration. That detail is what rewards a closer look through the phone. The church was badly damaged in 1812 and again in the Second World War. It served as a warehouse in Soviet times and was returned to the Vilnius Archdiocese in 2002. It is now also used for cultural events.

The best view is from S. Moniuškos skveras, the small square directly beside the church, facing the facade. From there you can fit both towers and the pediments in one frame, with the Moniuszko bust nearby as a foreground detail. Hold the phone upright for the towers. Keep it level, because tilting it up to fit the top makes the walls lean inwards. If you want a different view, Vilniaus gatvė shows the church within the Old Town streetscape, though it is the weaker of the two spots.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Vilnius Old Town. The square used for the photo, S. Moniuškos skveras, sits directly beside it.
text.directions_text: Start from the Old Town and head for S. Moniuškos skveras, the small square beside the church. If you are coming from further out, head to the Old Town and walk the last stretch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want both towers and the whole facade in one frame from the small square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pediments and the tower tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in S. Moniuškos skveras (the square directly beside the church, facing its facade). The church's Baroque facade and twin towers seen across the small square, with the Moniuszko bust nearby in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright so both towers fit. Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines, and keep the phone level to stop the walls leaning. Use the bust as a foreground detail, but don't let it block the doorway. For a second angle, try Vilniaus gatvė, where the church sits in the Old Town street scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight on an overcast day suits the pale detail well, and early in the day is usually quieter in the square.

text.access_note: The outside of the church can be photographed from the public square; the church is an active church and concert venue, so check opening hours before you go if you want to see inside.

name: Cathedral of the Theotokos, Vilnius
label: Orthodox Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Užupio tiltas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Užupio tiltas' (way/506335761): middle (26 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/343751993: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral of the Theotokos' (71 m across).
notes: Main Orthodox church of Vilnius with a bright facade.

text.description:
The Cathedral of the Theotokos is a Russian Orthodox cathedral, and it is one of the oldest church sites in Vilnius. The story goes back to 1346, when it was built for Uliana of Tver, the Orthodox wife of Grand Duke Algirdas. It has been burnt, rebuilt and put to other uses many times since. The university once used it as a library and an anatomical theatre. The look you see today comes mainly from the rebuilding of 1865 to 1868, which imitated medieval Georgian architecture. It was restored again after the Second World War and renovated in 1998.

It photographs well from the Užupis side of the Vilnia river. This is a simple, calm composition that works with any phone. Take one wide shot that includes the bridge, then step in with the zoom for the facade and its details. Another view along Rusų gatvė shows the cathedral from the street, if you want a second angle. Look at the screen before you shoot, because passers-by on the bridge can walk into the frame.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands at Maironio gatvė 14 in Vilnius, on the bank of the Vilnia river. The Užupis riverbank and Užupio tiltas are on the opposite side of the water.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or train stops near here, so head for Užupis, on the far bank of the Vilnia from the cathedral, or come by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped at Užupio tiltas and walk onto the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the cathedral across the river. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bridge and the riverbank in the frame. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for the facade and its details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Užupio tiltas (Užupis side of the Vilnia riverbank). The cathedral's fortress-like facade rising across the Vilnia river, framed by the bridge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the bridge as a leading edge at the bottom or side of the frame. Keep the cathedral in the upper two-thirds and keep the phone level so the walls stay straight. For a different view, try Rusų gatvė, where the cathedral appears along the street, or the corner of Maironio gatvė and Malūnų gatvė.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks too bright. Take a few shots in a row in case someone walks across the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the bridge.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship, but the view from the bridge is from a public place; check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

name: Church of St. Johns, Vilnius
label: St. Johns' Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Šv. Jono gatvė' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Šv. Jono g.' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24570013: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. John the Baptist and St. John the Apostle and Evangelist' (88 m across).
notes: Baroque church with the tall bell tower of the university.

text.description: St John's is the big Baroque church at the heart of the Vilnius University buildings in the Old Town, and its white bell tower is the real star for photographs. The tower is 69 metres tall, which makes it the tallest building in the Old Town, so it shows up above the rooftops from many streets. The church itself is older than its looks suggest. A Gothic parish church was finished here in the 1420s. After a fire in 1737 the architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz gave the front the flowing, wavy lines now seen as typical of Vilnius Baroque, and the tower was raised higher at the same time. The Jesuits received the church in 1571, and it became part of the university that grew from their college. It still hosts services in Lithuanian and concerts. For a phone photo, the challenge is height: the tower and church sit close together among narrow streets, so you need to tilt your view upwards without losing the shape. Stand in the street, find the tower rising behind the church's side, and use the gridlines to keep the edges upright. Move a few steps until the tower sits clear of wires and signs. If you want a second shot, the university courtyard shows the main front and tower together, and Pilies gatvė shows the side of the church along the old street.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Vilnius, within the Vilnius University ensemble. The viewpoint is on the small Šv. Jono gatvė, which runs off Pilies gatvė.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Vilnius Old Town and find Pilies gatvė. Šv. Jono gatvė is the small side street off it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower and the church together in a narrow street. If you can step back, try the default lens (1x) for a more natural shape. The telephoto (2x-5x) is good for the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Šv. Jono gatvė. The bell tower rising from the street, seen from the side with the church alongside it. The church is a short step to the north. Vilnius University Great Courtyard is an alternative: the Baroque front of the church is on one side, with the tall tower beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean. Keep some street at the bottom so the tower looks like it rises from it. For an alternative, Pilies gatvė shows the church's southern side, with its surviving Gothic windows, along the old street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the white walls keep their detail. Hold the phone level to avoid a leaning tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky is bright but the street is not crowded; early morning is usually quieter. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the pale tower.

text.access_note: The street is open public space, but the church is a place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet if you go in. Check the official site before you go for entry to the church, courtyard access and the bell tower, which is closed from roughly late October to April.
